title: Ardas at day's end
hook: many families close Rehras standing together in Ardas

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand at nightfall, and your line, joy at dusk. Did you notice the plate at dinner? Rehras has ended. Now, in many homes, everyone stands up. Day four hundred seventeen.

A front room in the evening. The last line of Rehras has been said. A grandmother puts her hands together and gets up from the sofa, a little slowly. The teenager looks up from her phone, sighs, and stands too. Somebody turns the TV off. The youngest boy stands on the cushion so he's taller. Nobody announces it. Everyone just knows: this is the part where we stand. Today: Ardas at day's end.
screen: `THE LAST LINE OF REHRAS.` → `A GRANDMOTHER STANDS; THEN EVERYONE.` → `THIS IS THE PART WHERE WE STAND.`

segments.voice: Ardas is the Sikh standing prayer. The word is usually traced to a Persian phrase for a petition, the kind of written request a subject would bring to a ruler. Sikhs say it standing, hands folded, often facing the Guru Granth Sahib if one is in the house. One person leads; the others listen, and say Waheguru together at certain points. It isn't a shabad from the Guru Granth Sahib. It's a prayer the community has said for centuries, with a standard form set out in the Sikh code of conduct. It opens by remembering: the ten Gurus by name, then the Guru Granth Sahib. Then the long line of Sikhs who kept faith, who served, who suffered and gave their lives, are brought to mind. Then comes the asking, for the whole community and for the world. And there's a place where a family can name tonight's particular reason: a grandfather in hospital, a new baby, an exam tomorrow, a safe journey. Then the close, said by Sikhs all over the world in the same words: Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa. In paraphrase: through Nanak's Name, may spirits rise; by Your will, may all be well. Not may we be well. May all be well. So the family in the front room ends the day by standing up for everyone, and naming the one or two people on their mind. Then, in many homes, the greeting: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Then they sit back down. Stand at day's end.
screen: `ARDAS: A PETITION, SAID STANDING.` · `REMEMBER: THE GURUS, THE SIKHS WHO KEPT FAITH.` · `NAME TONIGHT'S REASON.` · `SARBAT DAA BHALAA: MAY ALL BE WELL.` · then, large: `STAND AT DAY'S END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand for one minute's prayer. If you can, stand up now, feet steady, hands together in front of you. If you can't stand, sit up straight; that's fine. Bring to mind the people who carried you here: parents, teachers, anyone who kept faith before you. Then name one person on your mind tonight. If you pray, you can hold them before God in the plain words of your heart, or say Waheguru. Then widen it, the way Ardas does: may all be well. Stay there. The bell holds the time.
Ardas at day's end. The Sikh standing prayer that closes Rehras in many homes: remembering the Gurus and the faithful, naming tonight's need, and asking that all be well.
Your line: stand at day's end. Tonight, before bed, stand for a moment, think of one person, and widen it to everyone. Day four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Many Sikh families stand together for Ardas after Rehras, hands folded, one person leading and all saying Waheguru at set points; it ends with Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ardaas, the Sikh standing prayer, a petition.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ardas is just the Sikh word for any prayer.
what it means: a particular standing prayer that remembers the Gurus and the faithful, names a need, and asks that all be well.

what a scholar hears: the word is usually derived from Persian arz-daasht, a petition; the Rehat Maryada fixes a standard text that opens with the Tenth Guru's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, while the remembrance section has grown with Sikh history.

notes: Ardas structure (Gurus by name, the Guru Granth Sahib, remembrance of the faithful, petitions, a place for the specific purpose, closing line) is summarized, not quoted. Confirm.
Closing line transliterated and paraphrased: Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa. Confirm.
Etymology from Persian arz-daasht: phrased as 'usually traced'. Confirm.
The practice invites a person to hold someone 'before God in the plain words of your heart'; it does not supply a prayer text.
